title: Why Some Of This Retailer’s Leases Still Exist More Than 27 Years After It Filed For Bankruptcy
text:
Why Some Of This Retailer’s Leases Still Exist More Than 27 Years After It Filed For Bankruptcy 

### Service Merchandise filed for bankruptcy in March 1999 and all of its 350 Big Box stores closed; but 27 years later some of its store leases still exist—except other retailers occupy the spaces

Jason Miller

Mar 18, 2026

Service Merchandise filed for bankruptcy in March 1999.

At the time the Tennessee-based retailer had operated nearly 350 Big Box “catalog showrooms” throughout the country, mostly in Power Centers and some malls.

Thanks for reading Repurposed and redeveloped commercial real estate! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Service Merchandise closed 150 stores after it filed for bankruptcy.

All of its 200 remaining stores closed in 2002.

But even though Service Merchandise closed its stores nearly three decades ago, some of its leases still exist today—except that other retailers occupy the spaces.

How can leases to a defunct retailer still be in effect 27 years after its bankruptcy? 

The “value” that was in its leaseholds.

Service Merchandise was formally incorporated in 1960 as a catalog retailer with a single retail location in Nashville, Tennessee.

The Company ultimately evolved into a hybrid retail model in which sales were generated both via the ~600 page catalogs that it distributed to millions of customers each year and the retail showrooms that it opened throughout the country. 

The catalog and showrooms offered over 8,000 items including fine jewelry, housewares, small appliances, home electronics and other goods.

Service Merchandise ultimately grew to over 400 locations in 38 states by 1995.

The typical Service Merchandise store was ~50,000 square feet and situated alongside other retailers in large shopping centers.

The front of the store served as a showroom that displayed products for sale.

The remaining area was used as a stockroom that stored items and fulfilled orders placed by customers either in store or via the catalog.

While some high volume products were available on a self-serve basis, the majority of items were represented by a single sample on the showroom floor.

Customers carried a clipboard with a carbon paper order form, selected their desired items and, when complete, provided it to a clerk who processed payment.

The order was then submitted to the stockroom.

Small items would be loaded on a conveyor belt and delivered to a pick up area in the showroom while large orders could be picked up by pulling a vehicle around to the rear of the store.

This model—while unique in retail at the time—allowed customers to browse the store without a shopping cart and reduced the risk of theft and shrinkage. 

The Service Merchandise real estate strategy was to enter into ground leases for a term of 20 years or more with options to extend for another 20+ years.

These leases were generally at a low fixed rent and the extension options provided for minimal rent increases. 

Service Merchandise secured this low “ground” rent because it—and not the shopping center landlords—funded and constructed its buildings.

The majority of Service Merchandise leases were completed during the Company’s rapid expansion in the late 1970s and early 1980s. 

So when the Company went bankrupt in March 1999, more than 30 years of lease term and options remained on many of its leases.

These leases provided for rents of just $2.00 - $5.00 per square foot when the then-market rent was >5x that amount! 

In short, even though Service Merchandise the retailer was bankrupt, its leases had significant value.

Companies that file and operate in bankruptcy may terminate unexpired leases.

But instead of rejecting leases at many of its stores, the Service Merchandise bankruptcy estate continued to pay its existing lease obligations.

It then subleased this space to other retailers at rents that significantly exceeded the rent due to its landlords per the terms of its lease.

In bankruptcy, a debtor’s assets are auctioned to pay amounts owed to creditors.

Since the Service Merchandise leaseholds were an asset of its bankruptcy estate they were auctioned off to investors and users to raise funds for creditors.

Some landlords even paid to purchase their own leases to reclaim the space and complete new leases to other tenants at market rents. 

Other landlords sued to prevent sales to investors, claiming that they were prohibited by lease language.

Or that the leasehold acquirer did not provide “adequate assurance” to the landlord that it had a similar financial condition to that of Service Merchandise when it signed the lease—a requirement of the lease assignments.

In the end, most Service Merchandise leasehold sales were upheld. 

The new leasehold owners acquired the rights to the Service Merchandise leases and the market rate subleases that had been entered into with tenants such as TJ Maxx, HomeGoods, Michaels and DSW. 

These investors then collected market rents from subtenants, paid the low ground lease rent to landlords and captured the spread until the expiration of the Service Merchandise lease and extension option periods.

The Service Merchandise leasehold example is not a unique case.

Over the past decade many leaseholds that were held by now-bankrupt retailers such as Toys R Us, Sports Authority, Kmart, and the A&P grocery chain were also sold to investors and users in the course of each's bankruptcy process. 

More recently retailers have aggressively acquired the leaseholds of bankrupt companies to quickly and efficiently add new sites.

In fact, over 200 new retailer store openings in 2024 alone resulted from the lease acquisitions of just two bankrupt retailers—99 Cents Only Stores and Big Lots.

Dollar Tree DLTR 0.00%↑ acquired the designation rights for 170 store leases of discount retailer 99 Cents Only; these sites accounted for 1/4 of Dollar Tree’s 2024 new store openings.

Ollie’s Bargain Outlet OLLI 0.00%↑ acquired 8 leases of 99 Cents Only stores and 24 leases from the Big Lots bankruptcy in 2024.

Both Dollar Tree and Ollie’s acquired additional leases in 2025 following the bankruptcies of other retailers like Party City and Joann Fabrics. 

But perhaps no company has acquired more leases in recent years than off price retailer Burlington Stores BURL 0.00%↑: 

- In 2023 Burlington acquired 64 Bed Bath & Beyond leases; these sites accounted for ~40% of of its net new store openings in 2023 and 2024
- The following year Burlington Stores purchased 38 leases from the bankruptcy estates of 99 Cents Only, Big Lots and Conn’s HomePlus
- In 2025 Burlington acquired 45 leases from the Joann Fabrics’ bankruptcy estate; these sites may comprise ~40% of the retailer’s 110 net new store openings planned in 2026

And just last week Burlington bid $22 MM to acquire 22 leases of Saks Off Fifth, the off price division of Saks Global which filed for bankruptcy in January.

Once Burlington completes the acquisition of these leaseholds the former Saks Off Fifth sites will likely be part of its 2027 new store class.

Many of the bankrupt retailer leases acquired in recent years by Dollar Tree, Ollie’s, Burlington and others have substantial remaining lease and option term.

So just like with Service Merchandise, it would not surprise if the leases of bankrupt retailers 99 Cents Only, Party City and Joann Fabrics exist 27 years from now—even if other companies occupy the space.

Matthew McClintock

Mar 19

One of the best retail concepts ever. Great work on the history and remaining legacy.
